excerpt: Sharing what you are learning as you learn it: the post that asks a real question, how to answer people who know more, and the record that builds trust.

body.text: This lesson is about learning in public: sharing what you are building, asking real questions, and recording what you learn. You will learn what to post, what to keep private, and how the habit brings help from people you have never met.
Learning in public means showing the work while it is unfinished. It feels risky and it is useful, because the mistake somebody points out on Tuesday saves a week of guessing.
Before you start

items: One place you already post: a group, a forum, or a social account.
Something you are learning this month.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: What to share

items: The thing you built, even if it is plain.
The problem you hit, described in two sentences.
What you tried, and what happened.
The one question you cannot answer.
The resource that helped, with a line saying why.
A correction, when somebody shows you were wrong.

body.text: You will see the post get more replies when it contains a question than when it contains an announcement. People answer questions and scroll past news.

body.alt: A forum page with a question post and several replies.
body.caption: A specific question with the details attached. Vague posts get sympathy, and specific ones get answers.

body.text: It looks like you should wait until the work is good. Waiting means learning alone, and the people who could help are reading today.
How to ask so people answer

items: Say what you are trying to do, in one sentence.
Say what you tried, and what happened instead.
Include the error message exactly as it appeared.
Say what you have already read, so nobody repeats it.
Ask one question, not five.
Thank the person and post the answer that worked, so the next reader finds it.

body.text: The reply will often be a link rather than an explanation, and that is a gift. Follow it, try it, and then say whether it worked, which is the part most people skip.

body.alt: A small group with laptops at a community learning meetup.
body.caption: A room of people at the same stage. One evening there is worth a month of reading alone.

body.text: What stays private

items: Client work, unless you have written permission to show it.
Names, phone numbers, and anything from an identity document.
Screenshots that show a colleague's inbox or a customer list.
Anything said in a meeting that was not public.
Your own location, when you are working alone at night.
A mistake that would embarrass somebody else, even if it taught you a lot.

body.text: None of this limits what you share. The lesson is usually the method, and the method can be shown without the client's name.
Do not worry about posting something imperfect. A rough screenshot with a clear question teaches more than a polished post with nothing to ask.
Keep a record
A weekly note turns scattered practice into a track record you can show an employer.
The page will show the dates in order down the left side, which is what makes the notes a record rather than a memory. Read one month of them and you will see progress that the week itself hid.

items: Write three lines each week: what you tried, what broke, what you learned.
Keep the links to the posts and the answers.
Note the date, since a record without dates cannot be checked.
Photograph the finished thing, even if it is a page on a screen.
Every month, read the notes and choose one thing to go deeper on.
After six months, the notes are a portfolio with a story.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here happens to people who share their work, and each has a calm answer.

items: Nobody replies: the question was too broad, or posted where the wrong people gather.
Somebody is rude: answer once, politely, or say nothing. The thread is not the work.
You posted a client's name by mistake: delete it, tell the client, and check the screenshot rule.
You were wrong in public: post the correction, which raises your standing rather than lowering it.
You feel like an impostor: write the weekly note, which shows progress that memory hides.
The group is full of adverts: find one with moderators, even if it is smaller.

body.text: Practice
One question this week, and one note at the end of it.

items: Choose something you are stuck on.
Write the post with the three parts: aim, attempt, error.
Post it in one place where people do that work.
Try the first answer and reply to say what happened.
Write the three-line note before the week ends.

body.text: You can now learn with other people in the room. In the next lesson you will handle the client who stops replying after the work is done.

excerpt: What to do when a client delays, disputes, or disappears: the reminder that works, the documents to keep, and when to stop working.

body.text: This lesson is about the client who goes quiet: the late payment, the unanswered message, the dispute that arrives after delivery. You will learn a reminder that works, the records that settle an argument, and when to stop working.
Silence is not always bad faith. Sometimes it is a busy week, and sometimes it is a decision. A calm, written follow-up tells you which one you are dealing with.
Before you start

items: The quote, the messages, and the invoice for the job.
A bank statement showing what arrived.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: The first reminder

items: Wait until the agreed date has passed, then send one short message.
Repeat the invoice number, the amount, and the date it was due.
Ask one clear question: when will the payment be made?
Keep it to four lines, with no accusation in them.
Send it in the same thread as the quote, which holds the agreement.
Note the date you sent it, in case you need the sequence later.

body.text: You will see the message sit unread for a day and then a tick appear, which usually means it was seen. A seen message with no reply is information, and it changes the tone of the next one.

body.alt: A phone showing a polite payment reminder message with an invoice number.
body.caption: Four lines, one question, and the invoice number. A reminder that takes one reply gets answered.

body.text: It looks like chasing money ruins the relationship. Silence about money ruins it more slowly, and the written reminder protects both sides.
The second and third messages

items: After three days, send the same message with a date for the next step.
After a week, name the consequence written in your quote, such as pausing the work.
Offer a payment plan if the problem looks like cash flow rather than refusal.
Copy the person who introduced the client, if there was one.
Keep every message short, and never insult anybody in writing.
Stop sending after three attempts, and move to the next step.

body.text: The thread will become a record: quote, delivery, invoice, three reminders. That sequence is what a small claims process or a bank dispute asks for.
The screen will show the transfer with a date and a reference beside it, which settles the question in one screenshot. Send that screenshot with a single line, rather than an argument.

body.alt: A table with an invoice, a quote, and printed messages laid out in order.
body.caption: Quote, delivery, invoice, reminders, in date order. A dispute is settled by documents rather than by who is angrier.

body.text: When it is a dispute rather than a delay
A client who says the work is wrong is a different problem from one who has not paid. Answer the complaint first, then return to the money.

items: Ask which part is wrong, and what they expected instead.
Compare their answer with the quote, which may show a gap in expectations.
Offer one fix within the agreed changes, and price anything beyond it.
Put the agreement in writing again, so the next step is clear.
Do not withhold work that has been paid for, even in an argument.
If it cannot be settled, a written summary of the facts often ends it.

body.text: None of this needs a lawyer for a small job. Clear documents and a calm tone settle most of these before anybody else is involved.
Do not worry about being seen as difficult. A person who sends a polite reminder on time is easier to work with than one who stays silent and then explodes.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and the records are what make it possible.

items: The client says they paid: ask for the transfer reference and check your statement by date.
They paid part of it: acknowledge the part in writing, and restate the balance.
They ask for more work while owing money: decline until the balance clears.
They block your number: send the reminder by email, so the record continues.
The amount is small: decide whether the time costs more than the money, and say so in writing.
You have no written quote: send a summary of what was agreed now, and ask them to confirm it.

body.text: Practice
Prepare the messages before you need them.

items: Write the four-line reminder and save it as a template.
Write the second message, with the consequence named.
Check your quote actually states the consequence.
Build a folder for each client with quote, delivery, and invoice.
Note the day the next payment is due, in your calendar.

body.text: You can now handle silence without losing either the money or your temper. In the next lesson you will take on your first helper.

excerpt: Hiring your first helper: what to pay, what to write down, how to hand over work, and the mistake that costs a small studio its clients.

body.text: This lesson is about taking on your first helper, whether that is an apprentice, a part-time assistant, or a second freelancer. You will learn what to agree in writing, how to hand over work, and how to pay fairly.
A helper multiplies your time only if the work is handed over properly. Most first hires fail because the task was never described, not because the person could not do it.
Before you start

items: One task you repeat every week.
A written description of how you do it.
Two months of money to cover the wage, in case work is slow.

body.text: Start with one task

items: Choose the task that takes you longest and needs least judgement.
Write the steps as a list, as if for a stranger.
Do it together once, then watch them do it once.
Let them do it alone, and check the result the same day.
Add the second task only when the first is reliable.
Keep the decisions with you for the first three months.

body.text: You will see the first attempt take twice as long as doing it yourself. That is the cost of teaching, and it is paid once, unlike the task.

body.alt: Two desks side by side in a small room with two laptops.
body.caption: Two desks, one process. The second person works from your written steps, not from memory.

body.text: It looks like a bigger team means bigger clients. A team without written steps means more mistakes and the same amount of your time spent fixing them.
The agreement, in one page

items: The role, in three lines, and the tasks it covers.
The pay, the period it covers, and the day it is paid.
The hours, and whether extra hours are paid or swapped for time off.
Who owns the work produced, which should be you or the client.
Confidentiality, in plain words, since they will see client information.
How either side ends it, with notice measured in weeks.

body.text: The page will feel formal for a first helper, and it is the reason the relationship survives a disagreement. Two copies, both signed, one each.
The numbered list will show the two steps where people hesitate, and those are the ones to rewrite. A list with no hesitation points is ready to hand over.

body.alt: A person handing over an envelope of wages at a desk.
body.caption: Pay on the agreed day, every time. A helper who trusts the payday stays through the quiet months.

body.text: Pay and paper
Pay on time even when the client has not paid you, because your helper did the work for you and not for them.

items: Agree the amount before the first day, in writing.
Pay on a fixed day, by transfer, so there is a record.
Keep a simple record of days worked and amounts paid.
Pay for extra work rather than assuming goodwill.
Review the pay after three months, once you know what the work is worth.
Never pay late as a way of managing your own cash flow.

body.text: None of this needs a payroll service. A notebook with two columns, days and amounts, is enough until there are five people.
Do not worry about not being able to afford help. Start with a few hours a week on one task, which costs less than losing the client you cannot keep up with.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is common in a first year, and each has a straightforward answer.

items: The work is not right: check the written steps first, since the fault is often there.
They take shortcuts: make the checklist visible, and check the result for a week.
A client complains about them: answer the client, then speak to the helper privately.
They leave suddenly: the written steps are what let the next person start quickly.
Money is short in a quiet month: agree reduced hours in writing, rather than a late payment.
You are still doing everything: you hired for the wrong task. Choose a smaller one.

body.text: Practice
Write one process before you hire anybody.

items: Pick your most repetitive weekly task.
Write the steps as a numbered list.
Ask somebody to follow the list without your help.
Fix the two steps they got stuck on.
Save the list where you will find it again.

body.text: You can now grow without losing the quality that got you the work. In the next lesson you will weigh certificates against a record of finished work.

excerpt: What a certificate is worth to an employer, which exams count, and the record of finished work that beats paperwork on its own.

body.text: This lesson weighs certificates against a track record. You will learn what a certificate is worth in hiring, which exams are worth the fee, and how to build a record of finished work that answers the same question.
A certificate proves you attended and passed. A record proves you finished something somebody wanted, and employers increasingly ask for the second.
Before you start

items: A list of certificates you already hold.
One job advert in the field you want.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Read the advert first

items: Underline every qualification the advert names.
Note which ones say required and which say preferred.
Count how often a portfolio or experience is mentioned.
Check whether the certificate is named or the skill is described.
Compare across five adverts, so one employer does not set your plan.
Buy only the certificate that appears in most of the five.

body.text: You will see some adverts ask for a degree as a filter, which no certificate replaces. Others list skills, and those are the ones a portfolio can open.

body.alt: A study desk with a textbook, notes, and a practice exam paper.
body.caption: One exam at a time, with practice papers. The fee is worth it only when the advert names the certificate.

body.text: It looks like more certificates make a stronger application. A list of unrelated certificates reads as uncertainty, and one relevant certificate plus work reads as focus.
Exams worth the fee

items: Ones named in the adverts you are actually applying to.
Ones with a public syllabus, so you know what is being tested.
Ones with practice papers, which is how you pass.
Ones that can be renewed at a price you can afford later.
Ones from a body whose name an employer recognises.
Ones you can sit close to home, or online with a stable connection.

body.text: A cheap exam with an unknown body is money spent twice, since you will pay again for the recognised one. Check the body's name with three people in the field before paying.

body.alt: A framed certificate on a shelf beside finished project folders.
body.caption: The certificate sits beside the work, not instead of it. The folders are what an interview turns to.

body.text: The track record
A track record is a dated list of finished things, with the problem each one solved. It takes a year to build and it never expires.

items: Keep one page listing every finished piece, with the date.
Note the problem, what you did, and what changed.
Keep a copy of the work itself, where you are allowed to.
Ask each person you helped for one sentence you can quote.
Update the page monthly, which takes five minutes.
Bring the page to interviews, since most candidates bring nothing.

body.text: None of this needs a paid platform. One page, exported to PDF, opens on any employer's computer.
Do not worry if the record is short at the start. Three finished things with dates is already more than most applicants bring.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a normal part of building a career, and each has a practical answer.

items: You failed an exam: read the syllabus again, and sit it when you have practised the weak section.
The certificate expired: renew only if the adverts still ask for it.
An employer ignores your certificate: show the record instead, which answers a different question.
You cannot afford the fee: choose a free course with a project, and build the record first.
A course promised a job: check the advert, since employers do the hiring.
You have no work to show: volunteer one piece for a business you know, and date it.

body.text: Practice
Do the advert count before you spend anything.

items: Find five adverts for the job you want.
Underline every qualification in each one.
Count which certificate appears most often.
Start the one-page track record with three finished things.
Ask one person for a sentence you can quote.

body.text: You can now spend on learning where it counts. In the next lesson you will look at the shape of a working life, not a working week.

excerpt: Planning a working life rather than a working week: the seasons of a trade, saving for the quiet months, and the skills that keep paying.

body.text: This lesson is about the shape of a working life, rather than the shape of a working week. You will learn to plan for the quiet months, choose skills that keep paying, and decide what you want the work to give you.
Work has seasons. Every trade here has months of plenty and months of nothing, and a plan that assumes steady income is a plan that breaks in the quiet month.
Before you start

items: A notebook.
A rough idea of your income over the last year.
About twenty minutes, and honesty about the numbers.

body.text: Find your seasons

items: Write down your income for each month of the last year, from memory if needed.
Mark the three strongest months and the three weakest.
Look for the reason: school terms, holidays, harvest, or a client's budget.
Plan the quiet months for learning and for finding new clients.
Plan the strong months for saving, and for paying down what you owe.
Keep a small reserve that covers three months of costs.

body.text: You will see the pattern appear across a page, and it usually explains more than a monthly budget does. A year of figures turns worry into planning.

body.alt: A desk prepared in the morning with a notebook, a cup, and a laptop.
body.caption: A routine that survives a bad month. The work you can do half asleep is the work that keeps paying.

body.text: It looks like the answer is to work more hours. The answer is usually to work the same hours in a way that survives the quiet months, which is a different decision.
Skills that keep paying

items: Writing clearly, which every job needs and few people practise.
Numbers, at the level of a spreadsheet and a simple total.
Troubleshooting, which is patience applied to a problem.
Selling, which is explaining what you do so somebody can decide.
One technical skill, kept current rather than collected.
Teaching, because the person who can explain it gets asked again.

body.text: None of these go out of date in the way a tool does. Tools change, and the ability to write, count, and explain transfers to the next one.

body.alt: A signpost on a long road with several directions marked.
body.caption: A working life is several roads, not one. The skills above are the ones that travel between them.

body.text: Money for the quiet month
A reserve is the difference between a slow month and a crisis. It is built in small amounts, not in a good year.

items: Move a fixed share of every payment into a separate account.
Start with one week of costs, then one month, then three.
Do not treat the reserve as savings for a purchase.
Use it only when income stops, and repay it when income returns.
Review it twice a year, since costs rise quietly.
Keep it somewhere you can reach within a day.

body.text: The account screen will show a separate balance for the reserve, which is the whole reason for opening it. Look at that figure before you look at the main account.
Do not worry if the reserve is small at first. One week of costs already changes how a quiet month feels.
Deciding what the work is for

items: Write what you want the work to pay for, in plain terms.
Decide how many evenings a week are not for work.
Decide what you will refuse, such as work that needs your nights.
Check the decision once a year, since circumstances change.
Say it out loud to somebody who will remind you.
Change the plan when it stops fitting, rather than enduring it.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is normal over a long working life, and each has a step forward.

items: A quiet month empties the account: it is a planning gap, not a personal failure.
A good month is followed by spending: move the reserve first, then spend.
You are bored of the trade: teach somebody, which renews interest quickly.
The work has taken the evenings: choose one to protect, and hold it.
A tool you learned is obsolete: keep the skill underneath, which has not changed.
You cannot see a way forward: write the year's figures, since the pattern usually shows one.

body.text: Practice
One page of figures, one decision, one account.

items: Write your monthly income for the last year.
Mark the three strongest and three weakest months.
Name one reason for the pattern.
Open a separate account for the reserve, even with a small amount.
Write the one evening a week that stays free.

body.text: You can now plan a working life rather than survive a working week. In the next lesson you will check a result or an admission online without being charged for a free page.
